article_title: AI-Assisted Autonomous Learning and Reduced Academic Accomplishment in Vocational Higher Education: The Mediating Role of Hardiness
citation: Wang W and Zhang Q (2026). AI-assisted autonomous learning and reduced academic accomplishment in vocational higher education: the mediating role of hardiness. Front. Psychol. 17:1848291. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1848291
title: Psychological resource account of AI-mediated learning grounded in Self-Determination Theory
description: The article frames AI-assisted autonomous learning as a learning context that reshapes students' experiences of autonomy, competence, and challenge rather than merely a tool for efficiency. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory, it argues that when AI "functions as a scaffold" students retain ownership, but when it replaces effortful engagement, "the learning process may appear autonomous but become externally guided in substance." Hardiness (commitment, control, challenge) is positioned as the psychological resource transmitting these effects to academic self-evaluation, with Cognitive Load Theory as a complementary explanation for reduced deep processing.
requirements: Students must retain opportunities for independent decisions, effortful problem solving, and challenge appraisal for hardiness to be activated
constraints: The account is tested only cross-sectionally among vocational college students at one Chinese institution and the mediation is partial, so other mechanisms remain
target_learning_goals: academic adaptation and self-evaluated competence in AI-supported self-directed learning
examples: The study modeled AI-assisted autonomous learning as a second-order latent variable predicting hardiness and reduced academic accomplishment in an SEM
key_sources: Wang W and Zhang Q (2026). AI-assisted autonomous learning and reduced academic accomplishment in vocational higher education: the mediating role of hardiness. Front. Psychol. 17:1848291. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1848291

article_title: A study on AI-enabled course development, AI proficiency, and first-year students' academic and psychological adjustment
citation: Zhang J and Yin Y (2026). A study on AI-enabled course development, AI proficiency, and first-year students' academic and psychological adjustment. Front. Psychol. 17:1909803. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1909803
title: Course support–competence transformation–psychological outcomes framework integrating Self-Determination Theory and Control-Value Theory
description: The article constructs an analytical framework integrating Self-Determination Theory and Control-Value Theory to explain how AI-enabled course support relates to first-year students' self-reported psychological adjustment. It proposes that "course support → competence transformation → motivation activation → self-reported psychological outcomes" constitutes a coherent explanatory pathway, with AI proficiency as the mediating competence mechanism and AI usage pressure as a moderating boundary condition. Clear course structures are theorized to raise perceived control, while AI proficiency raises perceived competence.
requirements: Supportive course contexts with clear structures and effective guidance so that perceived control and competence can develop
constraints: The framework was tested only with cross-sectional self-report data, so all pathways are statistical associations rather than causal effects
target_learning_goals: Emotional management and stress coping in AI-supported courses
examples: The study tested the framework with hierarchical regression, bootstrap mediation, moderation, moderated mediation, and AMOS structural equation modeling on 551 first-year student responses
key_sources: Zhang J and Yin Y (2026). A study on AI-enabled course development, AI proficiency, and first-year students' academic and psychological adjustment. Front. Psychol. 17:1909803. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1909803

article_title: Empowerment over enforcement: unpacking the psychological drivers of AI-assisted deep revision in EFL writing
citation: Li, H. and Zhang, W. (2026). Empowerment over enforcement: unpacking the psychological drivers of AI-assisted deep revision in EFL writing. Front. Psychol. 17:1871022. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1871022
title: SDT-plus-Psychological-Safety integrated model of AI-assisted deep revision, scoped by Cognitive Load Theory
description: The article proposes an integrated framework in which Self-Determination Theory's psychological needs explain deep cognitive engagement with generative AI in EFL writing, complemented by Cognitive Load Theory: APL functions as "a strategic cognitive scaffold" that offloads lower-level linguistic operations, freeing working memory for higher-level reflection, which then supports Perceived Competence, Intrinsic Motivation, and Psychological Safety as parallel pathways to Deep Revision Engagement. Relatedness is deliberately dropped because the setting is solitary human-machine interaction, and Psychological Safety is introduced to capture the AI's "zero-judgment" low-stakes dialogic space.
requirements: The setting is solitary human-AI dialogic interaction rather than collaborative group work, justifying the narrowed focus on competence and autonomous motivation.
constraints: The model is tested with cross-sectional self-report data, so all pathways are interpreted as model-dependent indirect associations rather than causal links.
target_learners: Chinese university EFL learners in compulsory college English courses
target_learning_goals: Deep revision and autonomous text reconstruction in academic EFL writing
examples: The study tested the framework as a multiple parallel mediation model with PLS-SEM on survey data from 327 students.

article_title: Effects of generative artificial intelligence on students' learning motivation: evidence from a meta-analysis
citation: Fang L, Li Z, Xiong B and Lu Z (2026). Effects of generative artificial intelligence on students' learning motivation: evidence from a meta-analysis. Front. Psychol. 17:1832451. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1832451
title: Self-determination theory as the explanatory framework for GenAI's motivational effects
description: The article uses self-determination theory (SDT), which "distinguishes intrinsic motivation (IM), rooted in interest and curiosity, from extrinsic motivation(EM),drivenbyexternalcontingenciessuchasrewards and grades," as its coding scheme and explanatory lens. In the discussion, the authors propose that GenAI may support autonomy (individualized pathways, pacing), competence (diagnosing status, adjusting task difficulty, scaffolding), and relatedness (prompt responses, targeted encouragement), thereby fostering motivation. These mechanisms are offered as interpretations, not tested results.
requirements: Motivation outcomes must be classifiable as intrinsic or extrinsic motivation per SDT, as the article's coding scheme requires
constraints: The proposed need-supportive mechanisms are the authors' interpretation and were not experimentally tested in the meta-analysis
target_learners: students in formal educational settings from primary school through university
target_learning_goals: learning motivation, including intrinsic and extrinsic motivation
examples: The article coded motivation outcomes as intrinsic or extrinsic motivation guided by SDT, and interpreted the pooled positive effect through need support for autonomy, competence, and relatedness

article_title: Examining the Impact of Generative AI on Student Motivation and Engagement: The Mediating Role of Autonomy-Support and Autonomous Motivation in Education
citation: Ahmed A and Sultan A (2026) Examining the impact of generative AI on student motivation and engagement: the mediating role of autonomy-support and autonomous motivation in education. Front. Psychol. 17:1852265. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1852265
title: Integrated SDT–EVT–TAM framework for student engagement in GenAI-supported learning
description: The article proposes a unified framework combining Self-Determination Theory, Expectancy-Value Theory, and the Technology Acceptance Model to explain engagement in Generative AI-supported learning. It states that the study "extends existing AI-in-education literature by integrating SDT, EVT, and TAM within a unified framework to explain student engagement in Generative AI-supported learning environments." In the model, five perceived needs/value beliefs feed autonomy support for AI use and autonomous motivation for AI use, which drive student motivation and then engagement. The abstract reports that "autonomy support and autonomous motivation significantly increased student motivation, which subsequently emerged as the strongest predictor of student engagement."
requirements: Data from students with direct exposure to Generative AI tools, analysed via PLS-SEM with measurement and structural model evaluation
constraints: Tested in a single institution (King Saud University, Saudi Arabia) with a convenience sample; the article notes empirical evidence from Saudi higher education remains comparatively limited
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: student motivation and engagement in GenAI-supported learning
examples: PLS-SEM test of the integrated model with 297 students, with R² for engagement of 0.700
key_sources: Ahmed A and Sultan A (2026) Examining the impact of generative AI on student motivation and engagement: the mediating role of autonomy-support and autonomous motivation in education. Front. Psychol. 17:1852265. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1852265

article_title: From disengaged to self-determined: a latent transition analysis of students' AI learning motivation
citation: Liang, S., Yau, K. W., Meng, H., Chiu, T. K. F., King, I., Yam, Y., & Chai, C. S. (2026). From disengaged to self-determined: A latent transition analysis of students' AI learning motivation. Education and Information Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10639-026-13998-y
title: SDT-based five-indicator operationalization of AI learning motivation
description: The study extends Self-Determination Theory to AI education by operationalizing need satisfaction through five indicators: competence as confidence in learning AI (AICF) and perceived mastery of basic AI knowledge (AIKG), relatedness as AI for social good (AISG) and ethical use of AI (AIET), and autonomy as behavioral intention to learn AI (AIBI). As the article states, "Students' AICF and AIKG capture the competence dimension, as they reflect students' beliefs about their ability to understand and master AI concepts." All scales showed Cronbach's α ≥ 0.85 and full longitudinal measurement invariance was supported.
requirements: Validated self-report instruments for the five need-satisfaction indicators, rated on a 7-point Likert scale
Longitudinal measurement invariance across time points before comparing profiles
constraints: Relies on self-report measures of motivation, which the authors note may be subject to social desirability bias or limited metacognitive awareness
target_learners: Secondary school students (Grades 7–9) in AI education
target_learning_goals: Sustained motivational engagement in AI learning
examples: The framework was applied to 2,086 Hong Kong secondary students across a year-long AI curriculum using pre- and post-test surveys

citation: Ka Yan Fung, Tze Leung Rick Lui, Yuxing Tao and Kuen Fung SIN. (2025). MotiBo: The Impact of Interactive Digital Storytelling Robots on Student Motivation through Self-Determination Theory.
title: Self-Determination Theory as the framework for measuring storytelling engagement and motivation
description: The study frames its measurement of storytelling engagement and motivation in Self-Determination Theory, which the article describes as "a psychological framework that promotes intrinsic motivation and engagement in learning". A 14-question instrument was developed covering behaviour, emotion, cognition, and intrinsic motivation, with three questions dedicated to each area, administered as pre- and post-questionnaires around the five-day storytelling activities, supplemented by semi-structured interviews.
requirements: A 14-question instrument covering behaviour, emotion, cognition, and intrinsic motivation, with three questions per area, administered before and after the activities.
constraints: The framework was applied to five-day storytelling activities with young primary students in three modalities.
examples: An example questionnaire item is, "I find learning a story with [paper/PPT/robot] fun."

citation: Hidetake Tanaka, Hiroshi Igaki, Kazumasa Shimari, Kiyoshi Honda, and Naoki Fukuyasu. (2026). Practical Implementation Report on Introducing Spec-Driven Development Using AI Agents in Software Development PBL. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30572
title: SDD template project with copilot-instructions.md custom instructions and docs/ artifact directories for AI-agent workflow in SDPBL
description: A template project directory for Visual Studio Code distributed to each team to operationalize SDD in the course. citation: He Qian, Chang Guanglei, Su Ning, Yang Yingying, Ma Jun. (2026). Generative Artificial Intelligence Use and Learning Engagement Among Medical Undergraduates: Statistical Indirect and Configurational Associations Involving Basic Psychological Need Satisfaction. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16091694
title: Self-determination theory as a framework linking GAI use, psychological need satisfaction, and learning engagement
description: The article applies self-determination theory as its primary theoretical foundation, treating GAI use as a technology-related learning condition, basic psychological need satisfaction as a key learner-related psychological state, and learning engagement as a positive learning outcome. It states that "satisfaction of the needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness provides an important psychological foundation for autonomous motivation, sustained participation, and positive learning states." The framework motivates the combined SEM and fsQCA design and the expectation that similar levels of GAI use may accompany different psychological experiences and engagement levels.

constraints: The study measures general need satisfaction rather than need experiences specifically arising from GAI use
target_learners: medical undergraduates in clinical medicine-related programs
examples: The study modeled need satisfaction as a latent construct with autonomy, competence, and relatedness dimension scores as indicators, and used the three needs as fsQCA conditions

article_title: 'Artificial Intelligence in Online Education: A Systematic Review of Its Impact on Learner Engagement and Satisfaction'
citation: Ana Katalinic, Vanja Slavuj, Danijela Jaksic. (2026). Artificial Intelligence in Online Education: A Systematic Review of Its Impact on Learner Engagement and Satisfaction. Educ. Sci. 2026, 16, 389. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci16030389
title: Self-Determination Theory and the Technology Acceptance Model as explanatory frameworks for AI-supported engagement and satisfaction
description: The review frames learner engagement and satisfaction in digital environments through two named theories. Self-Determination Theory holds that "individuals are more motivated and actively engaged when their basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness are supported". The Technology Acceptance Model explains adoption through perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use; the review reports that when SDT needs are satisfied, learners perceive technologies as more useful and easier to use, increasing satisfaction and continued-use intention.
requirements: Application presupposes AI tools that support learners' needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness, and that learners perceive as useful and easy to use.
target_learners: higher education students in online courses
examples: The review cites empirical work reporting that satisfying autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs increases perceived usefulness, ease of use, satisfaction, and intention to continue using digital platforms.

article_title: How Can Bullying Victimisation Lead to Lower Academic Achievement? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Mediating Role of Cognitive-Motivational Factors
citation: Muthanna, Samara; Da Silva Nascimento, Bruna; El-Asam, Aiman; Hammuda, Sara; Khattab, Nabil. (2021). How Can Bullying Victimisation Lead to Lower Academic Achievement? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Mediating Role of Cognitive-Motivational Factors. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph18052209
title: Self-Determination Theory as the framework explaining how bullying victimisation undermines motivation and achievement
description: The article uses Self-Determination Theory (SDT) as its explanatory framework for why victimisation lowers achievement. SDT "postulates that relatedness, autonomy, and competence are three important factors to maintain positive well-being", and holds that all three needs must be supported for students to feel motivated and reach their academic potential. Negative school conditions such as peer rejection, social exclusion, and bullying may undermine these needs, offering a mechanism account for the mediation findings. The article also draws on expectancy-value theory and achievement goal theory as supporting accounts.
requirements: All three needs (relatedness, autonomy, competence) must be supported in students for motivation and achievement
constraints: The article notes the mechanism is supported by only a limited set of empirical mediation studies to date
target_learners: children and adolescents in school settings (ages 5-17)
examples: The meta-analysis tests the SDT-consistent prediction that victimisation reduces motivation and engagement, which in turn reduces achievement

article_title: The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective
citation: Frank Kellenberg, Joel Schmidt, Christian Werner. (2017). The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective. Signum Temporis 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1515/sigtem-2017-0001
title: Self-determination theory as a framework for designing adult training programs
description: Self-determination theory is a general theory of motivation standing in the humanistic tradition, in which the self interacts dialectically with its social environment. It postulates fundamental psychological needs for autonomy, competence and social integration whose satisfaction influences integration of experiences. The article applies it to the design of adult training programs, noting intrinsic motivation can be encouraged by freedom of choice but reduced by threats, deadlines, surveillance or rewards.
requirements: Learning environments must support the fundamental needs of autonomy, competence and social integration for motivation to be internalized
constraints: Intrinsic motivation can be reduced by circumstances such as threats, deadlines, self-observation, observation or assessment, and forms of rewards or feedback
examples: The article applies self-determination theory into the design of adult training programs with the goal of integration with self-regulation and reflective learning

description: The SDLE is a 110-item test designed to measure older adults' digital literacy level, divided into three sections: "Use and knowledge of the computer, Use and knowledge of the Internet and Knowledge of domestic and daily life devices." It was content-validated by a panel of 7 doctoral-level experts using Lawshe and Tristan's model, with items below the 0.58 cut-off eliminated (35 items removed from an initial 145). Scores map to competence levels from A+ (Total competence) to B (Low competence); the authors caution these are indicative, not absolute values.

article_title: Factors that explain simulation-based inquiry performance in physics learning
citation: Gerdesmann, D., Schwichow, M., & Koerber, S. (2026). Factors that explain simulation-based inquiry performance in physics learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09806-2
title: Extended SDDS framework: inquiry as structured search in hypothesis and experiment spaces
description: The Scientific Discovery as Dual Search framework describes inquiry as structured search in two interconnected spaces: a hypothesis space (divided by van Joolingen and de Jong into a variable space and a relation space) and an experiment space. The study maps cognitive factors onto these spaces: content knowledge constrains plausible hypotheses, CVS supports designing unconfounded experiments, and functional thinking supports reasoning about variable relations in the relation space. Seven measured inquiry facets were aligned to these spaces.
requirements: Guidance design requires knowing which cognitive skills support which inquiry facets within the SDDS spaces
constraints: The study applies the mapping in single-task, single-user digital simulation environments; the authors limit scope to such contexts
target_learners: young adults in physics inquiry learning
target_learning_goals: scientific inquiry skills including hypothesis generation, experiment design, and drawing conclusions
examples: The Cartesian diver task assessed seven facets spanning the variable, hypothesis, experiment, and relation spaces

article_title: Does inquiry-based learning work better in regular classrooms or computer-based settings?
citation: Hasan Ozgur Kapici. (2025). Does inquiry-based learning work better in regular classrooms or computer-based settings? Instructional Science (2025) 53:705–728. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09711-0
title: Self-determination theory framing of motivation quality in learning environments
description: The article adopts self-determination theory (SDT) as its motivation framework. SDT "differentiates the intensity and amount of motivation from the quality or type of motivation", refining the intrinsic/extrinsic split into "a distinction between autonomous (self-determined) and controlled motivation". Autonomous motivation arises when a learning environment satisfies needs for autonomy, self-efficacy (competence), and relatedness, and is associated with positive educational outcomes. The study assumed the virtual environment would support these needs, e.g. teachers refraining from disturbing interventions to provide psychological freedom.
requirements: A social context (learning environment) that satisfies learners' needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness to increase autonomous motivation
examples: The study assumed the inquiry-based virtual learning environment provided psychological freedom, self-efficacy, and a sense of belongingness; measured motivation nonetheless showed no group difference.

article_title: The more, the worse? The influence of the seductive detail amount on learning
citation: Lukas Wesenberg, Sebastian Jansen, Felix Krieglstein, Felicia Meusel, Sascha Schneider, Georg Valtin, Günter Daniel Rey. (2026). The more, the worse? The influence of the seductive detail amount on learning. Instructional Science (2026) 54:29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09781-8
title: Three cognitive-process accounts of the seductive details effect: distraction, disruption, and diversion theory
description: The article frames the seductive details effect within cognitive load theory and the cognitive theory of multimedia learning, which assume severely limited working memory. It details three mechanisms by which SDs exert extraneous processing: "Following distraction theory, the larger the amount of seductive content, the higher the probability that learners get distracted from the learning-relevant material." Disruption theory holds that longer interruptions impair mental organization of text segments, and diversion theory holds that thematically deviant SDs mislead learners about the overall gist. From this view SDs raise extraneous load and impair learning, predicting a dose-response relationship with SD amount.
requirements: The accounts assume limited working memory capacity, so overload likelihood rises with total cognitive load
constraints: The article notes prior evidence that SD effects can be mitigated by signaling, placement at the end rather than beginning, and marking SDs as learning-irrelevant
target_learners: students learning from texts with embedded interesting-but-irrelevant content
target_learning_goals: recall and transfer of learning-relevant text content
examples: The two experiments varied SD amount from 0% to 50% of the learning text while holding the number of interruptions constant to test the amount prediction derived from the three accounts
key_sources: Lukas Wesenberg, Sebastian Jansen, Felix Krieglstein, Felicia Meusel, Sascha Schneider, Georg Valtin, Günter Daniel Rey. (2026). The more, the worse? The influence of the seductive detail amount on learning. Instructional Science (2026) 54:29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09781-8

article_title: Fostering students’ motivation towards learning research skills: the role of autonomy, competence and relatedness support
citation: Louise Maddens, Fien Depaepe, Annelies Raes, Jan Elen. (2023). Fostering students' motivation towards learning research skills: the role of autonomy, competence and relatedness support. Instructional Science 51, 165–199. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09606-4
title: Self-determination theory and Basic Psychological Need Theory as a framework for motivation in complex-skill learning
description: The article adopts SDT (Deci & Ryan, 2000), which distinguishes amotivation, extrinsic (autonomous versus controlled) and intrinsic motivation, and maintains that "one should consider three innate psychological needs related to students' motivation": autonomy, competence and relatedness. Need satisfaction is hypothesized to relate to more internalized, autonomous motivation. The authors chose SDT precisely because its Basic Psychological Need Theory fits research-skills learning, where problems with both competence and autonomy feelings have been documented, and because van Merriënboer and Kirschner suggest it as the framework for motivation in 4C/ID contexts.
requirements: Operationalizations of each need drawn from existing research, as compiled in the article's overview of autonomy, competence and relatedness support
constraints: The article notes optimal circumstances for positive motivational outcomes require satisfaction of autonomy, competence and relatedness simultaneously, so single-need interventions may be insufficiently powerful
target_learners: upper secondary students learning research skills in academic contexts where learning is instrumental rather than voluntary
target_learning_goals: internalization of motivation towards learning research skills
examples: The need-supportive condition operationalized all three needs simultaneously via 12 implementations, testing the integrated-need-support hypothesis

article_title: Cultivating science data literacy in K-16 science education through data practices: A systematic review
citation: Jina Kang, Chungsoo Na, Morgan Diederich, Hillary Swanson, Lili Yan. (2026). Cultivating science data literacy in K-16 science education through data practices: A systematic review. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09803-5
title: Science data literacy framework of seven core data practices with associated facets
description: The review conceptualizes science data literacy (SDL) as enacted through seven core data practices: "understanding problems, designing experiments, collecting data, cleaning data, analyzing data, and evaluating and disseminating results, along with their associated facets". Each dimension is a high-level category (e.g., Analyzing Data) with specific facets (e.g., applying statistics, visualizing data), developed via inductive and deductive coding informed by NGSS and GAISE frameworks. SDL is framed as a multifaceted, iterative process rather than a linear sequence.
requirements: Studies must involve students engaging directly with data—gathering existing data, producing their own data, or using provided datasets for analysis
constraints: Framework derived from 42 peer-reviewed empirical studies in science education published 2001–2023
examples: The coding scheme clustered codes such as developing research questions under Understanding Problems and visualizing data under Analyzing Data, with inter-rater reliabilities reported per facet

article_title: Are children’s judgments of another’s accuracy linked to their metacognitive confidence judgments?
citation: Carolyn Baer, Puja Malik, & Darko Odic. (2021). Are children's judgments of another's accuracy linked to their metacognitive confidence judgments? Metacognition and Learning (2021) 16:485–516. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09263-x
title: SDT/Simulation Theory account of self- and other-oriented accuracy reasoning
description: The article tests a combined account in which Signal Detection Theory supplies the mechanism for confidence and Simulation Theory extends it to social reasoning. SDT holds that "confidence should be directly proportional to the degree of variability" of a decision, while Simulation Theory holds that "interpreting others’ mental states occurs through a simulation process, metaphorically putting oneself in another’s shoes." Together they predict strong self–other correlations when representations are shared, and that controlling for decision imprecision should eliminate those correlations.
requirements: Both judgments must be computed from the same, dimension-specific decision imprecision for correlations to appear
constraints: The account's predictions were not consistently supported: correlations appeared in only one of the first three experiments, and area accuracy did not predict social judgments
target_learning_goals: evaluating the reliability of one's own knowledge
evaluating the reliability of informants' knowledge
examples: Four experiments used area-discrimination tasks in which imprecision was experimentally manipulated by making shapes close in size (harder) or disparate (easier)

article_title: Self-Directed Learning in Problem-Based Learning and its Relationships with Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Loyens, S. M. M., Magda, J., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2008). Self-Directed Learning in Problem-Based Learning and its Relationships with Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-008-9082-7
title: SDL encompasses SRL: SDL is both learner characteristic and environment design feature, with learner control at task initiation
description: The article argues SDL and SRL share active engagement, goal-directed behavior, metacognition, and intrinsic motivation, yet cannot be used synonymously. SRL is usually a learner characteristic, while SDL is both a learner characteristic and a design feature of the learning environment. The decisive difference is control at task definition: "In SDL, the learning task is always defined by the learner", whereas in SRL the task can be teacher-generated. Hence "SDL can encompass SRL, but the opposite does not hold".
requirements: Conceptual clarity about what SDL entails so the terms are not used synonymously in research and practice
constraints: The distinction rests on the degree of learner control specifically at the beginning of the learning process when the task is defined
examples: In PBL, students formulate learning issues collaboratively after problem analysis, making the learner the initiator of the learning task

article_title: When is Learning “Effortful”? Scrutinizing the Concept of Mental Effort in Cognitively Oriented Research from a Motivational Perspective
citation: Axel Grund, Stefan Fries, Matthias Nückles, Alexander Renkl, Julian Roelle. (2024). When is Learning “Effortful”? Scrutinizing the Concept of Mental Effort in Cognitively Oriented Research from a Motivational Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09852-7
title: Self-Determination Theory account of effort-by-need frustration: aversive effort arises from frustrated needs for competence, autonomy, and relatedness
description: Within the article's framework, effort-by-need frustration is the negatively valenced affective-emotional experience of task execution, explained through Self-Determination Theory. SDT assumes three basic psychological needs — competence, autonomy, and social relatedness — whose satisfaction or frustration determines how attractive or aversive learning feels. The article states: "learning contexts can both foster and frustrate need satisfaction and consequently, can contribute to how attractive or aversive learning is experienced." For example, materials too easy or difficult for prior knowledge frustrate the need for competence, manifesting in aversion such as boredom, overload, or anxiety.
requirements: Learning environments must satisfy the needs for competence, autonomy, and relatedness to avoid aversive effort experience
constraints: Effort-by-need frustration is data-driven (arising from task execution) but is of a different kind than object-level processing requirements, with different psychological conditions of origin
target_learning_goals: reducing aversive learning experience and supporting autonomous motivation
examples: The article's homework vignette: a student reframed homework as a game, removing autonomy frustration while object-level requirements stayed the same

Basic Psychological Needs Under Constrained Autonomy: A Substantive–Methodological Reflection and Analysis of School Leaders' Needs from a Self-Determination Theory Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10079-3
title: SDT dual-process model of need satisfaction and frustration applied to constrained-autonomy leadership roles
description: The article applies Self-Determination Theory's dual-process model, in which need satisfaction and need frustration "are not merely opposite ends of a continuum; instead, they represent distinct processes", to school leaders operating under constrained autonomy—formal authority paired with limited discretion. Job resources are expected to feed primarily into need satisfaction and positive outcomes, whereas job demands feed primarily into need frustration and negative outcomes. School leaders are theorized as a boundary case that both crafts and experiences the climates they lead, making them a novel test of the model's generalizability.
requirements: Measurement must distinguish satisfaction from frustration as separate valence facets (e.g., the BPNSFS two-facet operationalization) rather than collapsing them into one continuum.
constraints: The article treats time methodologically (replicability across occasions), not as a basis for temporal or causal inference; findings are interpreted within the Australian school-leadership context.
target_learners: school leaders (principals and deputy/associate leadership team members)
target_learning_goals: understanding how workplace demands and resources shape leaders' motivation, well-being, and burnout through basic psychological need processes
examples: The study tested the model with 1,950 Australian school leaders using a two-wave survey and a nomological network of 64 workplace variables organized by the Job Demands–Resources framework.

article_title: Pathways to Student Motivation: A Meta-Analysis of Antecedents of Autonomous and Controlled Motivations
citation: Bureau, J. S., Howard, J. L., Chong, J. X. Y., & Guay, F. (2022). Pathways to Student Motivation: A Meta-Analysis of Antecedents of Autonomous and Controlled Motivations. Review of Educational Research, 92(1), 46–72. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211042426
title: Self-determination theory's motivational sequence: autonomy support → psychological need satisfaction → motivation quality
description: Self-determination theory explains student motivation along a continuum of motivation quality, from intrinsic motivation and identified regulation (autonomous motivation) through introjected and external regulation (controlled motivation) to amotivation. Its central premise asserts "a causal sequence that links autonomy support with enhanced psychological need satisfaction, which in turn fosters high-quality motivation, which in turn fosters adaptive outcomes." This meta-analysis systematically tested that sequence for the first time in education.
requirements: Need-supportive behaviors from notable others such as teachers and parents, namely "empathy, providing information, and supporting active participation", to satisfy students' psychological needs
constraints: The theory "makes no proposition about whether each need contributes equally or whether some will be more relevant than others"
target_learners: students from primary school to university
target_learning_goals: fostering self-determined (autonomous) academic motivation and reducing amotivation
examples: The meta-analysis tested the sequence with meta-analytic correlations, relative weight analysis, and W-COV GLS structural equation modeling across 144 samples

article_title: The Trans-Contextual Model of Autonomous Motivation in Education
citation: Hagger, M. S., & Chatzisarantis, N. L. D. (2016). The Trans-Contextual Model of Autonomous Motivation in Education: Conceptual and Empirical Issues and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315585005
title: Self-determination theory differentiates qualities of motivation, with autonomous forms most adaptive for persistence
description: Self-determination theory serves as the leading explanatory system in the model and distinguishes types rather than amounts of motivation: "The defining characteristic of the theory is that it differentiates between qualities or types of motivation experienced by individuals toward the activities and behaviors in which they engage rather than the quantity of motivation alone." Autonomous motivation (intrinsic, identified, integrated regulation) reflects acting with choice and volition, while controlled motivation (external, introjected regulation) reflects externally referenced contingencies. Basic psychological need satisfaction (autonomy, competence, relatedness) and internalization are the mechanisms by which autonomous motivation develops and persists.
requirements: Satisfaction of the three basic psychological needs (autonomy, competence, relatedness) underpins optimal functioning and autonomous motivation
target_learning_goals: self-regulated participation in and persistence with educational activities

article_title: Adolescent flourishing in a digitally connected world: A qualitative systematic review and meta-synthesis
citation: Gordon, C. S., Brake, N., Hammond, S. P., Picton, I., Notley, T., Rowston, K., Gutierrez, A., Basarkod, G., Costello, K., Gupta, M., West, M., & Dicke, T. (2025). Adolescent flourishing in a digitally connected world: A qualitative systematic review and meta-synthesis. Preprint. https://osf.io/j48k5/?view_only=8b6423082746439abb4106526e953aaf
title: Self-Determination Theory framework organising adolescent digital flourishing into autonomy, competence, and relatedness themes
description: The review uses Self-Determination Theory as the organising framework for synthesising adolescents' positive online experiences. "Guided by the tenets of Self-Determination Theory, the analysis generated ten subthemes organised under the core categories of autonomy, competence, and relatedness." SDT holds that individuals flourish when basic psychological needs for autonomy (agency and self-endorsed action), competence (mastery and effectiveness), and relatedness (connection and belonging) are met. The synthesis presents these dimensions as interconnected, displayed in a layered concept map showing fluid, overlapping relationships between subthemes.
requirements: Qualitative studies capturing adolescents' own narrative accounts, with at least two meaningful participant quotes
constraints: The review focuses on adolescents aged 12–19 and on positive experiences, explicitly not denying negative experiences but balancing a deficit-focused conversation
target_learning_goals: wellbeing and flourishing in digitally connected learning and social contexts

article_title: Gamification on Mathematics Engagement and Motivation in Secondary School and Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Ratinho, E., Figueiredo, M., Estêvão, D., Faísca, L., & Martins, C. (2026). Gamification on Mathematics Engagement and Motivation in Secondary School and Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10108-1
title: Self-Determination Theory as the dominant motivational framework for gamification, complemented by ARCS, SCT, AGT, and Flow Theory
description: The review organizes gamification's motivational effects through established frameworks, with Self-Determination Theory the most frequently used (n = 13), followed by SCT (n = 8) and the ARCS model (n = 6). Under SDT, "the satisfaction of autonomy, competence, and relatedness is essential to fostering intrinsic motivation", and game elements can be aligned with these needs: points and levels support competence, avatars and team leaderboards support relatedness, and task choice supports autonomy. The review argues controlling or comparative elements may undermine autonomy and competence, while feedback, scaffolding, and self-paced progression tend to support basic psychological needs.
requirements: Gamified designs must be aligned with students' psychological needs (autonomy, competence, relatedness) rather than adding elements superficially
constraints: The review notes a recurring reliance on non-validated or ad hoc measures of motivation, often with limited theoretical grounding, which restricts comparability across studies
target_learners: Secondary and higher education students in mathematics courses
target_learning_goals: Sustaining motivation and engagement in mathematics learning
examples: Points and levels framed as progress feedback for competence; team leaderboards for relatedness; task or difficulty choice for autonomy

article_title: What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis
citation: Emma C. Burns · Penny Van Bergen. (2025). What Are Teacher–Student Relationships in Adolescent Motivation Research? A Systematic Review of Conceptualizations, Measurement, and Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09998-y
title: Self-determination theory frames relationships via relatedness support, alongside autonomy support and structure as distinct needs-supportive practices
description: SDT is a meta-theory spanning development and motivation, arguing that optimal motivation requires three psychological needs: autonomy, competence, and relatedness. "In classrooms, needs can be met through teachers' provision of autonomy support (i.e., asking student opinions, offering choice, providing explanatory rationales), structure (i.e., instructional guidance, clear expectations), and relatedness support (i.e., care, warmth, also referred to as involvement)". Relatedness support is the only explicitly relational component; autonomy support and structure reflect more unidirectional dynamics and are not intended as relationship measures.
requirements: Approaches using autonomy support or collective needs support as relationship indicators should disentangle interpersonal aspects (e.g., trust, respect) from pedagogical aspects (e.g., offering choice)
constraints: Relatedness support is relatively under-researched compared to autonomy support and structure, and there is very little research regarding relatedness thwarting
target_learning_goals: Supporting students' autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs to foster academic motivation
examples: Some researchers have used autonomy support as an indicator of relationship quality, arguing autonomy supportive behaviors capture ongoing patterns of interpersonal dynamics

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective
citation: Evans, P., Vansteenkiste, M., Parker, P., Kingsford-Smith, A., & Zhou, S. (2024). Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09841-2
title: Self-determination theory as an integrative framework linking cognitive load theory and motivation
description: The article proposes self-determination theory as a unifying motivational framework for cognitive load theory research, which has historically studied motivation with unitary constructs or no unifying framework. SDT contributes two key mechanisms: fulfillment of the basic psychological needs of "competence, relatedness, and autonomy," and a motivation continuum "from amotivation, an absence of motivation, through controlled motivation... to autonomous motivation." The study operationalizes these via the relative autonomy index and teacher motivating styles, showing that strategies supporting autonomous motivation also minimize extraneous load.
requirements: Adoption of multidimensional motivation measures (e.g., the SDT motivation continuum) rather than unitary motivation constructs
constraints: The article makes no claims about whether one motivation theory should be preferred over another; basic psychological need experiences were not measured in the present study
target_learning_goals: self-regulated motivation and engagement in school subjects
examples: The study computed a relative autonomy index from the Self-Regulation Questionnaire-Academic and modeled engagement as behavioral, emotional, cognitive, and agentic factors.

citation: Hospel, V., & Galand, B. (2016). Are both classroom autonomy support and structure equally important for students’ engagement? A multilevel analysis. Learning and Instruction, 41(1), 1-10. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.09.001
title: Self-determination theory as the framework linking teacher autonomy support and structure to student engagement
description: The study is carried out "within the framework of self-determination theory", which the authors use to organize two distinct classroom-level teacher provisions — autonomy support and structure — and to investigate their "specific, additive and combined effects" on students' behavioral, cognitive and emotional engagement. The framework treats the learning environment as a classroom-level context whose provisions relate differentially to engagement components, with structure linked to all three and autonomy support to emotional engagement.
requirements: Both teacher provisions are measured as students' perceptions at the classroom level, requiring aggregation across students within classes
constraints: Evidence concerns ninth-grade students in language classes; the abstract does not generalize beyond this setting
target_learning_goals: behavioral, cognitive and emotional engagement in classroom learning
examples: 744 ninth-grade students from 51 classes completed a questionnaire about their engagement during language classes and their perceptions of the teacher's provision of autonomy support and structure

article_title: It is autonomous, not controlled motivation that counts: Linear and curvilinear relations of autonomous and controlled motivation to school grades
citation: Mouratidis, A., Michou, A., Sayil, M., & Altan, S. (2021). It is autonomous, not controlled motivation that counts: Linear and curvilinear relations of autonomous and controlled motivation to school grades. Learning and Instruction, 73, 101433. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2020.101433
title: Self-Determination Theory quality-of-motivation account of academic achievement
description: Self-Determination Theory distinguishes autonomous motivation — acting out of interest, enjoyment, or personal importance (intrinsic and identified regulation) — from controlled motivation — acting under internal or external pressure (introjected and external regulation). The article applies SDT's key proposition that "high quality of motivation (i.e., high autonomous motivation and low controlled motivation) which matters for positive outcomes" to school grades, testing it with polynomial regression. Autonomous motivation is said to foster an internal locus of causality and fuller recruitment of inner resources, while controlled motivation produces a less adaptive mode of functioning.
requirements: Measures distinguishing autonomous (intrinsic + identified) from controlled (introjected + external) regulation, validated via higher-order CFA in each sample
constraints: Formulated and tested here for Turkish adolescent students in middle and high school using the Self-Regulated Questionnaire tradition; recent findings (Phillips & Johnson, 2018; Brunet et al., 2015) have cast partial doubt on the incongruence tenet in other domains
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement as reflected in school grades in mathematics and Turkish language
examples: Both samples' motivation was measured with translated Likert scales; grades came from school records rather than self-report to reduce common method bias

article_title: Longitudinal associations between academic motivation and school-related stressors in adolescents transitioning to secondary school
citation: Wang, J., Kaufman, T., Mastrotheodoros, S., & Branje, S. (2025). Longitudinal associations between academic motivation and school-related stressors in adolescents transitioning to secondary school. Learning and Instruction, 98, 102144. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102144
title: Self-Determination Theory account of controlled and autonomous academic motivation shaped by relationships with parents, peers, and teachers
description: The article organizes its hypotheses with Self-Determination Theory, under which individuals regulate behavior along controlled and autonomous orientations: "Controlled motivation is often associated with external pressures and rewards, while autonomous motivation is characterized by self-determination and intrinsic drive." Relationships Motivation Theory, a mini theory of SDT, supplies the mechanism: people have an innate need for connection and belonging, so stressors from parents, peers, and teachers can create an unsupportive environment that shifts motivation toward controlled or away from autonomous forms.

Measurement of adolescents' subjective perceptions of relationship quality with parents, peers, and teachers
constraints: The study assesses adolescents' subjective perceptions via self-report, which the authors note may reflect perceptual biases or shared method variance rather than actual differences in parental or teachers' behaviors
target_learners: adolescents transitioning from primary to secondary school
target_learning_goals: academic motivation (controlled and autonomous regulation of academic behavior)
examples: The study tested SDT-derived hypotheses by correlating growth factors of three school-related social stressors with growth factors of controlled and autonomous motivation across four waves spanning the secondary school transition

article_title: Do children’s executive functions account for associations between early autonomy-supportive parenting and achievement through high school?
citation: Bindman, S. W., Pomerantz, E. M., & Roisman, G. I. (2015). Do Children's Executive Functions Account for Associations Between Early Autonomy-Supportive Parenting and Achievement Through High School? Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000017
title: Self-Determination Theory-based account: autonomy-supportive parenting fosters executive functions via autonomous motivation and practice on challenging activities
description: The article draws on Self-Determination Theory to explain why autonomy-supportive (vs. controlling) parenting may build children's executive functions. It argues that "when parents support children's autonomy rather than attempt to control children, they foster children's fulfillment of the basic need for autonomy," producing autonomous rather than controlled motivation. Autonomously motivated children are proposed to sustain engagement in challenging activities that require executive functions, practicing and strengthening these skills; autonomy support may also foster language skills used in self-talk for inhibition and switching. The study tests this account's prediction that early autonomy support predicts later executive functions and achievement.
requirements: Parenting must be ongoing over time; the article states brief interludes of autonomy support are unlikely to suffice for developing executive functions
constraints: The account is tested with correlational longitudinal data, so causal conclusions are not possible per the article
target_learners: children from infancy through high school
target_learning_goals: executive functions (inhibition, delay of gratification, sustained attention)
academic achievement in math and reading
examples: The study combined observations of autonomy support at 6, 15, 24, and 36 months into a single index, reflecting the argument that support must be ongoing

article_title: Relation between teachers' early expectations and students' later perceived competence in physical education classes: Autonomy-supportive climate as a moderator.
citation: David Trouilloud, Philippe Sarrazin, Pascal Bressoux, Julien Bois. (2006). Relation between teachers’ early expectations and students’ later perceived competence in physical education classes: Autonomy-supportive climate as a moderator. Journal of Educational Psychology, 98, 75-86. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.98.1.75
title: Self-determination theory account of autonomy-supportive climate as a moderator of social influence on students
description: The article applies self-determination theory (Deci & Ryan, 2002) to the teacher-expectations paradigm. It defines an autonomy-supportive climate as "a motivational style including behaviors such as offering choices, encouraging independent problem solving, involving students in the decision process, and minimizing the use of pressure". Because such climates enhance self-determination, students in them are theorized to be less susceptible to conforming to social factors such as teachers' expectations, whereas controlling climates reduce self-determination and increase susceptibility. The study used this framework to derive its moderation hypothesis.

examples: The study measured students' perceptions of the autonomy-supportive climate with a French version of the Learning Climate Questionnaire (α = .75) aggregated to the classroom level (Rwg = .65 to .80), then tested the climate as a cross-level moderator of teacher expectation effects.

article_title: Teacher motivational strategies and student self-determination in physical education.
citation: Taylor, I. M., & Ntoumanis, N. (2007). Teacher motivational strategies and student self-determination in physical education. Journal of Educational Psychology, 99, 747-760. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/

Self-determination is determined by satisfaction of three innate psychological needs—autonomy, competence, and relatedness—and teachers' motivational strategies (autonomy support, structure, involvement) map onto these needs in a social-contextual sequence tested in this study.

citation: Julie Boiché, Philippe Sarrazin, Frederick Grouzet, Luc Pelletier, Julien Chanal. (2008). Students’ Motivational Profiles and Achievement Outcomes in Physical Education. Journal of Educational Psychology, 100 (3), pp.688-701. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.100.3.688

The framework shifts the unit of analysis from global motivation to the configuration of motivation types a student holds.
requirements: Requires measurement of the separate SDT motivation types rather than only a global self-determination index, so that combinations can be detected via cluster analysis.
constraints: Studied in the domain of physical education (gymnastics teaching cycles) with high school students.
target_learners: high school students in physical education
target_learning_goals: motor skill performance and achievement in physical education
examples: Cluster analyses in the two studies yielded self-determined, non self-determined, and moderate profiles among gymnastics students.

article_title: Why grades engender performance-avoidance goals: The mediating role of autonomous motivation.
citation: Pulfrey, C., Buchs, C., & Butera, F. (2011). Why grades engender performance-avoidance goals: The mediating role of autonomous motivation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(3), 683–700. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0023911
title: Self-determination theory's perceived-locus-of-causality framework as the mechanism linking grading to avoidance goals
description: The article uses the perceived-locus-of-causality framework at the heart of self-determination theory to explain why grading breeds avoidance. The framework "organizes reasons for acting into a range going from controlled to autonomous", with controlled motivation comprising external and introjected regulation and autonomous motivation comprising identified and intrinsic regulation. The authors argue that graded evaluation places students in dependence and powerlessness vis-à-vis the teacher who controls the valued resource, reducing autonomy, and that this erosion of autonomous motivation renders performance-avoidance, rather than performance-approach, goals salient.
requirements: The account presupposes that the student perceives the grade as dispensed by an external controlling authority on whom the grade's value depends.
constraints: The account is developed for normative, grade-based evaluation in classroom settings; the experiments were carried out in Swiss professional schools.
target_learners: secondary and postsecondary students in graded courses (Swiss professional school students, ages ~15–30)
target_learning_goals: motivational quality of engagement (autonomous versus controlled motivation) and pretask achievement goal adoption
examples: Experiment 3 measured autonomous motivation with the Reported Autonomy Index after a graded or nongraded exercise and tested it as a mediator of subsequent performance-avoidance goal adoption.

article_title: Analyzing the network structure of students’ motivation to learn AI: a self-determination theory perspective
citation: Jiajing Li, Jianhua Zhang, Ching Sing Chai, Vivian W. Y. Lee, Xuesong Zhai, Xingwei Wang & Ronnel B. King. (2025). Analyzing the network structure of students' motivation to learn AI: a self-determination theory perspective. npj Science of Learning 10:48. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00339-w
title: Self-determination theory as a framework for students' AI learning motivation
description: The article applies self-determination theory (SDT) to AI education, treating motivation as having both quantity and quality. Based on degree of internalization, "SDT differentiates intrinsic motivation, identiﬁed regulation, introjected regulation, external regulation, and amotivation." SDT further posits that fulfillment of three basic psychological needs — autonomy, competence, and relatedness — fosters more internalized motivation, and that environmental factors such as social support and facilitating conditions act as catalysts. The study extends SDT into AI-infused learning and argues motivation should be studied as an intertwined dynamic system rather than as isolated variables.
requirements: Application requires measuring qualitatively distinct motivation types and basic psychological needs satisfaction, which the study did via validated multi-item Likert scales with internal consistency from 0.78 to 0.95.
constraints: The study notes its findings on need centrality refine SDT in the AI context specifically; the sample was all Chinese university students, which the authors say may explain introjected regulation's centrality.
target_learners: university students learning with and about AI
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement and motivation in AI learning
examples: The study operationalized the five motivation types with the AI Motivation Scale (four items per subscale) and needs satisfaction with three items each, then mapped them as network nodes.

citation: Benneker, I. M. B., Lee, N. C. & van Atteveldt, N. (2023). Mindset and perceived parental support of autonomy safeguard adolescents' autonomous motivation during COVID-19 home-based learning. npj Science of Learning 8:4. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00153-2
title: Self-determination theory's three basic psychological needs as a framework for predicting autonomous motivation during home-based learning
description: The article applies self-determination theory, which "proposes that humans have three fundamental needs that must be satisfied in order to achieve complete autonomous motivation: autonomy, relatedness and competence." It operationalizes autonomy as perceived parental autonomy support, relatedness as positivity of parent-adolescent interaction, and competence as self-efficacy, and tests them as predictors of adolescents' autonomous motivation during COVID-19 school closures alongside mindset theory.
requirements: Measures of all three needs appropriate to the home-based learning context, including dyadic parent and adolescent reports
constraints: In this study only the autonomy need (parental autonomy support) was supported; relatedness and competence measures did not significantly predict motivation
Data are observational, so the framework's predictive roles were tested without causal inference
target_learners: Dutch early adolescents in secondary school (mean age ~14.45 years)
target_learning_goals: Maintaining autonomous (intrinsic and identified) motivation for schoolwork during home-based learning
examples: Stepwise regression on 76 parent-adolescent dyads testing the three needs as predictors, controlling for pre-pandemic motivation and parent demographics

title: Design online mathematics courses with self-check buttons, prior knowledge sections, and chunked scaffolding to support competence
description: The article recommends three design features for improving competence in online mathematics courses: self-check buttons with informative and correctness feedback, prior knowledge explanations with self-check practice, and content chunking with scaffolding. These features are grounded in both quantitative and qualitative findings and are being integrated into the school's new Algebra 1 course.

constraints: Recommendations should be considered in light of specific context variations and requirements due to limited purposive sampling

title: SDT-based digital needs support framework crossed with the three-phase SRL cycle for designing ChatGPT learning activities
description: The article organizes ChatGPT-based learning design around self-determination theory, which "suggests three innate needs: autonomy, relatedness, and competence," crossed with the social cognitive SRL model of three iterative phases: forethought, performance, and self-reflection. Digital needs support means designing digital learning environments to satisfy these needs; the study applies the framework to classify which ChatGPT activities satisfy which need and foster which SRL phase from a teacher perspective.

examples: The framework structured the Delphi survey: teachers indicated which SDT needs and SRL phases each candidate ChatGPT activity primarily impacted.

description: Because assessment guides and evaluates self-directed learning, the authors recommend that educators "develop and implement appropriate assessment strategies that align with the goals and objectives of SDL initiatives." They specify that this "could include formative assessments, self-assessment tools, and peer evaluation methods." This principle addresses the alignment between assessment design and SDL pedagogy rather than a tested comparative result.

title: Self-Directed Learning as a theory of andragogy
description: The article frames Self-Directed Learning as "a theory of andragogy in which adult learners take their own initiative to identify and tailor their individual learning process and outcomes." It traces the theory to Garrison (1997), building on Malcolm Knowles' theory of andragogy, and specifies that SDL "requires the capacity to identify learning needs, select resources for learning, implement learning strategies and assess the outcomes achieved." In undergraduate medical education, SDL is operationalized through students formulating their own learning goals.
requirements: Learners must be highly motivated, team players, with problem-solving and time management skills, and equipped to source and filter relevant information from quality sources, per the authors.
constraints: SDL was applied to a limited subset of topics within undergraduate medical curricula in the reviewed studies, which the authors note may skew perceptions of its effectiveness.
examples: The review's included studies implemented SDL through formats such as case-based learning, problem-based learning, e-learning modules, and simulation-based training.

article_title: Self-directed learning in health professions: A mixed-methods systematic review of the literature.
citation: Berger-Estilita, Joana; Linda, Krista; Gogollari, Artemisa; Schmitz, Felix; Elfering, Achim; Guttormsen, Sissel (2025). Self-directed learning in health professions: A mixed-methods systematic review of the literature. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0320530
title: Thirteen SDL models and frameworks applied in healthcare organizations, classified as personal, process, context, and combined models
description: The review identifies thirteen SDL models applied across twelve included studies, classified into "four combined models, five process models, three context models, and one personal model." Named models include Knowles' model on self-directed learning, Deci and Ryan's Self-Determination Theory, Zimmerman's Self-Directed Learning Theoretical Model, Karasek's Job Demands-Control model, Marsick and Watkins Models for Informal and Incidental Learning, and Tynjälä's 3P Model, among others. The review reports that only about one-third of included studies explicitly used or referenced such models, and that "a unified SDL model tailored to clinical settings remains absent."
requirements: Models must be adapted to the dynamic nature of roles and responsibilities among healthcare professionals, as the review finds a one-size-fits-all solution impractical.
constraints: The review states the challenges in creating a universal SDL model stem from the dynamic nature of roles among healthcare professionals, and that frameworks originating from sectors like business and technology require adaptation toward patient-centered outcomes, ethical practice, and clinical safety in healthcare.
target_learners: Healthcare professionals including nurses, pharmacists, and physicians
target_learning_goals: Understanding and applying SDL models in clinical and workplace learning contexts
examples: The review's Table 1 describes each model's type, description, and context of use, such as Cuyvers' Self-Regulation of Professional Learning model applied to nurses' self-regulated workplace learning in clinical wards.

title: Self-Determination Theory as the framework explaining how bullying victimisation undermines motivation and achievement
description: The article uses Self-Determination Theory as its explanatory framework for why victimisation lowers achievement. SDT "postulates that relatedness, autonomy, and competence are three important factors to maintain positive well-being", and the authors argue that negative school conditions such as peer rejection, social exclusion and bullying may undermine these needs, reducing motivation and aspirations, which in turn impairs academic achievement. Expectancy-value and achievement goal theories are cited as complementary accounts.
requirements: All three needs — relatedness, autonomy and competence — must be supported in students for them to feel motivated and achieve their highest academic potential, as the article states.
constraints: The article presents SDT as an interpretive framework supported by prior studies, not as a mechanism tested within the meta-analysis itself.

examples: The authors interpret the meta-analytic mediation result through SDT: bullied students feel less connected to school, present lower academic motivation and reduced perceived academic competence, and lower educational aspirations than non-bullied peers.

article_title: Teacher Autonomy Support: Does It Hinder Motivation among Thai Students?
citation: Amrita Kaur, Rosna Awang Hashim & Mohammad Noman. (2014). TEACHER AUTONOMY SUPPORT: DOES IT HINDER MOTIVATION AMONG THAI STUDENTS? Malaysian Journal of Learning and Instruction, Vol. 11, 171-189. http://mjli.uum.edu.my/
title: Self-determination theory: autonomy support as the crucial teacher behavior for high-quality motivation
description: Self-determination theory explains motivation and its quality through social contextual variables that, when supported, sustain high-quality motivation. It holds that "humans are naturally motivated to engage in activities that are volitional or self-chosen", and that autonomy means actions that are self-endorsed with an internal perceived locus of causality — not independence, since a person can rely on others for guidance and still feel autonomous. In classrooms the construct becomes teacher autonomy support, which the article operationalizes through Reeve and Jang's instructional behaviors and tests experimentally in Thai classrooms.
requirements: Teachers must extend autonomy support through classroom contexts, refraining from controlling language and threatening assessments
constraints: The article notes the construct's significance has been challenged by cross-cultural researchers claiming collectivist values diminish the need for autonomy
target_learners: Thai grade-6 students in public school English classes
examples: The study operationalized TAS via an intensive teaching module adapted from Reeve et al. (2004), with the experimental teacher undergoing three training sessions of approximately 60-80 minutes

Its core component is an Early Warning System that "uses student attendance and course performance data, along with teacher observations on other local factors associated with school-leaving, to identify students at highest risk of dropping out of school." examples: In Cambodia, one treatment group received the EWS alone while a second received computer labs and computer literacy training in addition to the EWS

description: The article integrates Self-Determination Theory and Social Cognitive Theory to explain how digital technology use improves English performance. constraints: The framework was tested in a cross-sectional design with senior high school EFL students in one Chinese region
examples: The study's theoretical model (Fig. 1) positions emotional intelligence and learning engagement as serial mediators between digital technology use and English academic performance

description: The article proposes a conceptual framework in which SDL (self-management, learning desire, self-control), PsyCap ("self-efficacy, hope, optimism, and resilience"), and CIT (interdisciplinary teaching design, implementation, evaluation) are second-order constructs linked in a mediation model. It draws on "the theory of adult learning", psychological capital theory, and the iceberg competency model, which distinguishes visible competencies (knowledge, skills) from hidden ones (self-concept, traits, motives). requirements: Measurement of all three constructs via validated multi-dimensional questionnaires with five- or six-point Likert scales
constraints: The model includes no moderating variables, as the authors found insufficient theoretical and empirical support for moderation in the primary paths

title: Self-determination theory's four-type motivation continuum applied to interpersonal motivation in collaborative learning
description: The article applies self-determination theory's continuum of self-determination to motivation for interpersonal relationships in collaborative learning, distinguishing external regulation (rewards, punishment, coercion), introjected regulation (shame and anxiety), identified regulation (perceived value or importance), and intrinsic motivation (interest, fun, enjoyment). It developed a 16-item questionnaire assessing these four concepts for the question of why students want to be close to group members, and reports that "In the first study to assess interpersonal motivation for collaborative learning, the role of identified regulation was shown to be especially important." The framework organizes the study's path model from motivation through engagement to performance.
requirements: A validated questionnaire distinguishing the four motivational concepts for interpersonal relationships in collaborative learning
constraints: The study states little prior research has examined interpersonal motivation in collaborative activities from the self-determination theory perspective
target_learners: university students in lecture courses incorporating collaborative learning
examples: Participants answered items such as "Because it is important for me to spend time with group members" (identified) and "Because it is fun to spend time with group members" (intrinsic) before the lecture
key_sources: Ito Takamichi, Umemoto Takatoyo. (2022). Examining the causal relationships between interpersonal motivation, engagement, and academic performance among university students. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0274229

article_title: The effectiveness of simulation education program on shared decision-making attitudes among nurses in Taiwan.
citation: Lin Mei-Hsiang, Lin Shu-Chuan, Lee Yu-Hsia, Wang Pao-Yu, Wu Hon-Yen, Hsu Hsiu-Chin. (2021). The effectiveness of simulation education program on shared decision-making attitudes among nurses in Taiwan. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0257902
title: SDMA and SPS OSCE rating scales for shared decision-making attitudes in end-of-life care
description: The authors developed two OSCE rating instruments because no existing tools applied: the examiner-scored SDMA scale, with 12 questions across "empathic communication and mastery learning" on a three-point scale (maximum 24, Cronbach's α = .80), plus a one-item five-point SDMA global score; and the standardized-patient-scored SPS scale, five questions on empathy and communication (α = .80) plus a one-item four-point global score. Five experts with over 10 years' clinical experience reviewed both, giving a content validity index of 1.00.
requirements: Examiners and SPs complete training and rehearsal to ensure standardized scoring; examiners' joint evaluation of training videos showed Cronbach's α of .90
constraints: Developed specifically for EOL SDM teaching situations; validated with five experts at one medical center
target_learning_goals: attitudes toward shared decision-making in end-of-life care
examples: Used by blinded examiners and standardized patients to score every participant in the two-month post-intervention OSCE

title: SDMA cultivation program: two-week lecture plus Three Talk video-based EOL simulation intervention
description: The intervention evaluated in the study was a two-week SDM attitude cultivation program for nurses, comprising weekly sessions of three hours of SDM basic-concept lectures and three hours of video-based simulation teaching. Its video simulations referenced Elwyn et al.'s Three Talk model and were produced in "appropriate" and "inappropriate" versions covering three EOL scenarios: choice talk about receiving or not receiving intensive care, option talk covering pros, cons and patient preferences, and decision talk following the decision. Faculty members with more than five years of EOL clinical experience led all phases.
requirements: Videos in paired appropriate/inappropriate versions per scenario; faculty registered nurses with over five years' EOL experience
constraints: Evaluated only as an add-on to normal practice, with participants at a single hospital where SDM is an accredited skill with on-service training
target_learners: clinical nurses at a medical center in Taiwan

SDM communication with patients and families

title: Incorporate SDM components into EOL-care simulation when designing nursing education programs for shared decision-making attitudes
description: The authors conclude that simulation programs for end-of-life care should incorporate SDM components, arguing that "simulating EOL care with SDM could be an effective strategy for training clinical nurses and improving their attitudes toward SDM." They position the evaluation as a reference for nursing-administration managers designing SDM-related education programs and for incorporating SDM into clinical nursing curricula, even though the measured between-group attitude differences were not statistically significant.

constraints: The measured effect on SDM attitudes was not statistically significant; sample was from a single hospital with possible selection bias and cross-contamination

article_title: The Influence of Teachers on Motivation and Academic Stress and Their Effect on the Learning Strategies of University Students.
citation: Trigueros R., Padilla A., Aguilar-Parra J.M., Lirola M.J., García-Luengo A.V., Rocamora-Pérez P., López-Liria R. (2020). The Influence of Teachers on Motivation and Academic Stress and Their Effect on the Learning Strategies of University Students. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17239089
title: Self-Determination Theory as a framework for teacher influence on student motivation and stress
description: The article applies Self-Determination Theory, described as "a macro theory of human motivation that suggests the significant influence of the social context on human behaviour". Within it, teacher influence is a duality: autonomy support, which "encourages self-determined motivation and student engagement in the classroom", versus psychological control, which "encourages controlled motivation and hinders the student's commitment". SDT also posits a motivational continuum from autonomous motivation through controlled motivation to demotivation. The study uses this framework to model how teacher behaviour relates to academic stress, motivation, learning strategies and performance in university students.
requirements: The framework requires measuring students' perceptions of teacher autonomy support and psychological control, here via validated questionnaires
constraints: The article notes most prior SDT studies analysed only teacher behaviour and motivation, with few linking teacher behaviour to student psychological distress such as stress
target_learning_goals: use of metacognitive strategies and critical thinking
examples: The study modelled teacher autonomy support and psychological control as exogenous predictors of academic stress in a structural equation model with 2456 university students
